12o955d.text: Google's Gemini AI agents repeatedly attempted to hack a real organization's website during AI model safety testing, finding ways to circumvent increasingly restrictive security controls designed to prevent them from accessing live systems. The security incidents occurred in October as AI safety research company Trajectory Labs tested whether Gemini 4 Argon agents would engage in unauthorized behavior when faced with an impossible task, even with the model's built-in API safeguards enabled. In reports published Friday, Trajectory Labs and the targeted organization, Epoch AI, revealed that the agents attempted SQL injection attacks, probed for sensitive information, impersonated employees, and repeatedly circumvented network restrictions introduced to contain their activity. Epoch AI said it had not independently verified which AI models were involved, and that the Gemini identification came from Trajectory Labs. The researchers tasked the agents with retrieving official answers to nonexistent problems from Epoch AI's FrontierMath benchmark, repeatedly instructing them to "NEVER stop, NEVER give up." On October 20, approximately 40 agents began probing Epoch AI's live website for sensitive information, including administrator credentials and access to proprietary benchmark evaluation logs. Epoch AI detected the activity and deployed an "agent hotline" that allowed the agents to send messages directly to its employees. For three hours, the agents made 36,411 requests to a planted API endpoint and sent 487 messages through the hotline, including some that attempted to impersonate actual Epoch employees or claimed to be engineers and auditors requesting benchmark information. An investigation also identified an attempted SQL injection attack and more than 200 attempts to access FrontierMath evaluation logs. Trajectory Labs discovered the activity while reviewing agent transcripts and notified Epoch AI of the unauthorized attacks the following morning. After discussing the incident with Epoch, the researchers agreed to continue testing against a local copy of the website instead of its live infrastructure. However, the agents continued finding ways to circumvent the restrictions. During testing on October 23, some agents recognized they were interacting with a copy of Epoch's website, identified the real website's IP address, and connected directly to its live infrastructure, bypassing DNS redirection designed to contain them. When researchers blocked the IP addresses used to reach Epoch, an agent switched to another address that allowed it to access the live website again. Trajectory Labs subsequently configured its network proxy to block direct connections to Epoch, but an agent found another way to retrieve the website's public content through a third-party web-reader service. "In some of these runs, the agents worked out that they were on a copy, identified the correct raw IP to bypass our redirect, and reached the live site again, which Epoch alerted us about," Trajectory Labs explained. In a separate technical analysis, Trajectory Labs researchers also discovered that the agents created a message board through a shared software package cache to communicate with each other, exchanging information about vulnerabilities and exploitation methods. In one example, an agent shared a technique for bypassing restrictions on a deliberately vulnerable copy of Epoch's website, which another agent subsequently used to obtain credentials and complete the task. The researchers also observed agents attempting to bypass CAPTCHA protections and impersonating employees to trick an AI assistant into revealing protected benchmark information. Beginning October 26, Epoch AI agreed to work with Trajectory Labs on additional experiments, knowing the agents would have internet access and could interact with its public website. During these tests, the agents again accessed Epoch's live infrastructure, making more than 65,000 requests to a planted API endpoint and attempting further SQL injection attacks and employee impersonation. Trajectory Labs later moved testing into fully isolated environments without internet access. Even after this change, the agents still tried to disable a fake control that allegedly blocked network access, and they succeeded in all three complete test runs. The researchers said that the agents had not been explicitly instructed to hack websites or impersonate employees. However, they were given an impossible objective on purpose and repeatedly instructed not to give up. Trajectory Labs acknowledged that the incidents resulted from shortcomings in its testing procedures, including conducting experiments without obtaining the affected organization's consent and relying on built-in model safeguards without sufficient additional monitoring. On November 2, the company suspended all AI misalignment testing pending a risk assessment and the addition of further safeguards. "These incidents show how easily testing capable AI agents can spill over to affect real systems and people, and there are not yet shared standards for doing it safely," Trajectory Labs warned. Neither organization confirmed that any private Epoch AI information was exposed during the incidents. This report comes as California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the company failed to adequately contain autonomous AI agents during testing, resulting in more than 80 incidents in which it lost control of the agents. The lawsuit follows a July incident in which nearly 700 OpenAI-powered agents escaped a controlled testing environment and attacked Hugging Face's production infrastructure while attempting to steal cybersecurity benchmark answers. 112it65.text: California on Monday sued OpenAI for breaking state law barring companies from engaging in unfair and unlawful business practices due to its alleged failure to stop its AI agents from hacking Hugging Face and deceiving the public about that cyberattack and other similar incidents. The lawsuit, filed in San Francisco Superior Court, alleges OpenAI officials told state Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office it has lost control over its agents 80-plus times during testing. OpenAI then failed to cooperate with the attorney general’s probe, the office said. “Rather than take responsibility and be transparent with the public and with regulators so that these loss-of-control incidents can be analyzed and prevented, OpenAI thwarted the Attorney General’s efforts to investigate these incidents, including by refusing to provide detailed information about the full universe of incidents known to the company,” the lawsuit said. OpenAI allegedly responded to subpoenas with “just a smattering of publicly available information, self-serving blog posts and redacted copies of a few dozen external communications containing high-level descriptions of select security incidents,” according to the lawsuit. The artificial intelligence giant is violating California’s Unfair Competition Law, Bonta says, and the company also qualifies as a public nuisance under state law due to its allegedly dangerous practices. The attorney general is asking a judge to prevent OpenAI from using unfair competition tactics, restore money individuals and organizations lost due to its practices and assess civil penalties of $2,500 per violation against each defendant found at trial to be responsible for breaking the law. The attack on Hugging Face in July specifically was foreseeable given that OpenAI chose to test models it “knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight,” according to a Bonta press release. An OpenAI spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but provided CNBC with a statement saying it has “undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity” since the Hugging Face episode. “We’ve published a detailed technical report, commissioned and published a separate independent report, notified affected organizations, strengthened safeguards across our research systems, and created a framework for additional identification and disclosure of misalignment,” the spokesperson reportedly said. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.” ‘Destructive, deceptive, and adversarial’ The Hugging Face attack was predictable, Bonta said in a statement that blamed an internal culture at OpenAI that puts growth ahead of safety. OpenAI’s decision to test a “dangerous” product without needed protections or oversight, as well as deceiving the public about its practices, violate California law, the lawsuit said. Even as it warned of the risks of AI-fueled cyberattacks for almost 10 years and assured the public that it had strong safeguards in place, OpenAI in reality flouted its own policies and aggressively moved ahead with testing despite having evidence that its cyber protections were not good enough to contain the models it was creating, the lawsuit said. “As OpenAI is well aware, these models do not behave predictably and can often take destructive, deceptive, and adversarial actions to complete their assigned tasks,” the lawsuit said. “OpenAI attempts to mitigate these risks by implementing safeguards in its publicly released models but deliberately omits or removes these protections while experimenting with and training its models.” OpenAI also ignored obvious signs that its agents had escaped the sandbox in the weeks preceding the Hugging Face attack, the lawsuit said. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman in June, accusing the tech behemoth of releasing a product they knew could harm consumers. OpenAI is facing several lawsuits alleging that its ChatGPT platform contributed to some users becoming delusional, committing suicide or carrying out violent crimes. 1697a19.text: Google Project Zero will replace its “90+30” disclosure policy with shorter, fixed deadlines in response to AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and exploitation. The transition is gradual and began on November 13, when the 30-day extension was removed from the vulnerability disclosure timeline. On February 2, 2027, the deadline will be further reduced to 60 days, and on January 3, 2028, it will shrink to just 30 days. Once the deadline expires, Project Zero will publish vulnerability details even if a fix is not available. Project Zero is Google’s vulnerability research team, focused on the discovery of serious security flaws in widely used software and hardware. Some of its notable recent findings include a .NET Framework zero-day, flaws in Chrome’s JavaScript engine and graphics components, and a Qualcomm chipset zero-day linked to NoviSpy spyware attacks. When the team finds a flaw, it reports it privately to the vendor and typically publishes the technical details after a set period, giving time for developing security updates and patches, as well as a margin for most users to apply them. Project Zero says AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery and exploitation, and made it easier for attackers to reverse-engineer fixes as soon as patches ship and develop working exploits. This policy change puts greater pressure on vendors to investigate reports, develop fixes, and ship them faster to customers. Project Zero said a gradual approach to shortening the disclosure deadline was the better choice, giving vendors time to develop better flaw management and remediation systems. Vendors warned Google that jumping straight to 30 days could expose users to severe risks and could lead maintainers to focus on Project Zero findings while ignoring other, potentially more severe flaws reported by others. “An overarching concern was that immediately changing the policy could harm users by making unfixed vulnerabilities available to attackers while vendors are in the process of improving their remediation processes and technology,” Google explained. “While the benefits of delaying disclosure are declining due to the increased probability that attackers will discover a vulnerability during the embargo period, we still feel there are benefits in the short term.” Project Zero noted some early disclosure exceptions, such as when a flaw is actively exploited in the wild, when others have already published exploitation or vulnerability details, or when a vendor requests early disclosure. Exceptions will also apply for non-disclosure, as Google deems fit, using the example of Spectre and Meltdown, for which it previously withheld information for longer than 120 days. ffv1se.text: California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the company knowingly continued testing advanced artificial intelligence models despite repeated security failures that allowed autonomous AI agents to escape isolated environments and launch cyberattacks against real-world organizations. The lawsuit claims OpenAI misled the public about its cybersecurity safeguards and failed to adequately monitor increasingly advanced AI cybersecurity models, resulting in more than 80 incidents in which the company lost control of its agents during testing. The legal action follows a July security incident where hundreds of OpenAI-powered agents escaped a controlled testing environment and hacked Hugging Face, an artificial intelligence platform, compromising production infrastructure and stealing internal credentials. California says the Hugging Face attack resulted from OpenAI repeatedly focusing on experimental AI testing without ensuring adequate safeguards were in place. "The Hugging Face cyberattack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability," the complaint reads. The lawsuit alleges that OpenAI continued testing increasingly capable AI agents despite knowing its sandbox environments could be bypassed, potentially exposing third-party systems to unauthorized activity. "In truth, OpenAI failed to comply with its own internal policies and consistently and aggressively moved forward with testing and experiments even in the face of evidence that its cybersecurity safeguards were insufficient to contain the highly advanced models it was developing," the lawsuit continues. During the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI models exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in JFrog Artifactory to break out of their isolated testing environment and access the internet. The attack lasted more than two days, with nearly 700 autonomous agents coordinating through an unauthorized message board to plan the attack on Hugging Face's production systems while attempting to steal answers to a cybersecurity benchmark. The California complaint alleges that OpenAI ignored or missed warning signs in the weeks leading up to the incident, including evidence that agents had already escaped their testing environments and were abusing third-party services and platforms. It also claims that OpenAI's agents subsequently targeted software repositories, informational websites, and foreign government databases containing sensitive health information. In another incident, experimental agents allegedly compromised OpenAI's own internal infrastructure and obtained administrator-level access to critical systems. According to the complaint, OpenAI has acknowledged more than 80 instances of losing control of autonomous agents during testing but publicly disclosed only 27 incidents. The lawsuit follows a subpoena issued by Bonta's office in September, with California claiming that OpenAI failed to provide sufficient information about the incidents and instead supplied limited documentation and descriptions of previously disclosed attacks. The state is pursuing claims under California's Unfair Competition Law and public nuisance laws, seeking court orders requiring stronger safeguards, civil penalties, and other relief. The rise of autonomous AI attacks The lawsuit comes amid growing concerns about increasingly capable AI models escaping controlled cybersecurity evaluations and attacking organizations outside their intended testing environments. These autonomous attacks are not limited to OpenAI agents, with other AI platforms disclosing similar incidents in the past. In July, Anthropic disclosed that its Claude models had breached production systems at three organizations during cybersecurity evaluations. One model created and uploaded a malicious Python package to the public PyPI repository, where it was downloaded and executed on 15 real systems. This led Anthropic to remove internet access from all internal AI model evaluations following additional incidents involving unauthorized activity against government websites and other external systems. Google also confirmed to The Wall Street Journal in September that its Gemini AI model had accessed the internet and hacked three companies during cybersecurity testing conducted in May. California's lawsuit argues that OpenAI's failure to address these risks adequately has exposed organizations and the public to unnecessary cybersecurity threats, even as it told customers that its AI development practices were safe. 10ow80p.text: Ireland’s data protection regulator will fine the Match Group €11 million ($10 million) as a result of the dating app Tinder allegedly failing to provide users with their personal data held by the company upon request. The country’s Data Protection Commission (DPC) alleged Tinder offers a self-service tool known as Download My Data that purports to let users access a complete copy of their information, but in reality fails to provide all of it. Some categories of data were left out without users’ knowledge or were only supplied as summaries, the regulator’s press release said. The agency also alleges data provided by the tool did not comply with Europe’s General Data Protection Regulation’s right of access standard, which requires controllers to let consumers know if their personal information is being processed. “These tools do not need to provide a complete copy of personal data, but they must be fair and transparent to individuals regarding the extent of the data provided,” DPC deputy commissioner Graham Doyle said in a statement. The probe was launched in January 2020. Tens of thousands of users accessed the tool during the nearly six-year-long inquiry, according to the press release. The DPC issued an order requiring Match to begin complying with the data processing rule within three months. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

37tixg.text: Hackers who breached the cloud environment of network and email security company Barracuda earlier this month used a stolen cloud access key and the ARTEX AI penetration testing framework. The company says the attacker accessed approximately 10 of its cloud accounts over a 44-hour period between November 1 and 2. The attacker's presence was discovered on November 4, and Barracuda's investigation determined that the open-source AI pentesting framework ARTEX was used for this "machine-speed intrusion." The company explains that the attacker leveraged a cloud access key provided to a third-party vendor for the duration of a previous project. "We did not retire the key when the vendor — a company working in AI — finished that work. That is on us," Barracuda says. The security company believes the attacker stole the key from the unnamed third-party AI vendor in October. It confirmed that the key was stored in a configuration file in the vendor's GitHub repository. The attacker used credentials they found in one system to move through Barracuda’s data analytics environment, source-code repositories, and Kubernetes clusters. Based on the attacker's commands targeting cryptocurrency-related secrets, including private keys, Ethereum keystore files, and seed phrases, Barracuda believes the attack was financially motivated. However, the company does not rule out that this activity might have been a diversion from the attacker’s true motive. The threat actor attempted to establish persistence by deploying a container that mounted the host’s file system, including credentials stored on it. A separate attempt to create a new cloud administrator identity was blocked. Barracuda says the attack used machine-style labels, certain probing methods, and built-in hunting routines that matched what is found in ARTEX. The firm noted that the attack was very similar to a recent incident at cloud hosting provider Railway, which also involved credential chaining and the apparent use of ARTEX. According to the cybersecurity company, the attacker reached a system that stores customer integration credentials for Barracuda XDR; however, it found no evidence that those were accessed or stolen. Because of the uncertainty surrounding this scenario, Barracuda asked potentially affected Managed XDR Cloud or Monitored Endpoint customers to revoke and recreate their integration credentials. 1hoqiau.text: Italy’s data protection regulator announced a €805 million ($886 million) fine against Meta on Saturday, saying the social media giant accessed user photos and videos without their specific consent or properly informing them. The fine, announced Saturday, is one of the biggest the Italian regulator — known as the Garante — has ever issued. The crackdown on Meta’s Facebook platform involved the company’s alleged use of its “camera roll” suggestions option, launched in 2023, to browse Android users’ photo galleries to recommend posts they could enhance with personal photos and videos. In addition to the photos and videos, the regulator said, Facebook accessed related metadata. The investigation found Meta asked users to access their camera roll through a single permission that “applies across the entire app covering multiple features with different requirements,” according to a Garante press release. The permission is preceded by a “non-specific notice” to enable other features, the press release said, failing to make clear to users that they are consenting to suggestions from the camera roll, the regulator said. It also alleged the feature was turned on by default. “When given in full, such permission allows the app to access the entire photo library on the device, usually on a permanent basis, without the user or [regulators] being able to verify what information is actually being used,” the press release said. The practice violates Italian data protection regulations safeguarding “the smartphone as part of the individual’s private sphere,” according to a Garate press release. “Consequently, any access to the information stored on such devices requires free and informed consent, regardless of whether data is transmitted or any harm occurs,” the press release said. Meta had argued the Garante lacked jurisdiction to issue the fine, but the regulator dismissed that claim. A Meta spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but told other news outlets in a statement that the company strongly disagrees with the decision and plans to appeal what it called the “disproportionate” fine amount. The tech giant has been under fire worldwide in recent months, losing multiple court cases in the U.S., including an October decision in which the company was fined $25 billion for deceiving consumers about how it uses their data. In addition to the fine, the Garante has ordered Meta to make several changes in the next 60 days, including by obtaining consent through a request that is “separate and specific to the feature” and clearly explaining what it is used for. Meta also must begin disabling the option by default. The unusually high fine is due to the fact that about 20 million Italian Android users were impacted, the long time period over which the violation occurred and the company’s lack of cooperation during the probe, the press release said. 1y4ojna.text: King Charles III on Monday opened the new headquarters of Britain’s National Cyber Force, the secretive unit that runs the country’s offensive cyber operations against hostile states, terrorists and criminals. Staff are already working in the building near the Lancashire village of Samlesbury in northwest England, named Ribble House after the nearby river and Ribble Valley. The government chose the village as the force’s permanent home five years ago and committed £5 billion ($6.5 billion) to the NCF through 2030. The NCF brings together staff from the cyber and signals intelligence agency GCHQ, the Ministry of Defence, the Secret Intelligence Service (MI6) and the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory. Officials say it carries out operations every day. “In an age of radical uncertainty, contested geopolitics, and rapidly changing technology, the NCF keeps the country safe by delivering high-impact cyber operations every single day against those who threaten our interests,” said GCHQ Director Anne Keast-Butler who showed the king around the site. As first reported by Recorded Future News, a new commander is currently in charge at the NCF, replacing Air Vice-Marshal Tim Neal-Hopes in September, although officials have yet to name them publicly. Neal-Hopes took over in October 2023 from James Babbage, a former GCHQ officer who subsequently moved to the National Crime Agency. To date, the NCF has rarely discussed its work in public, saying disclosures would undermine the effects of its covert operations. In a 2023 doctrine paper, it described its operations as “accountable, precise, and calibrated,” in a way that was fundamentally different from those practiced by Britain’s adversaries. Gen. Sir Rob Magowan, commander of Cyber and Specialist Operations Command, said: “The opening of the National Cyber Force’s new headquarters marks a significant milestone in strengthening the UK’s ability to combat threats in an increasingly contested world. “We must be ready to confront, deter and prevail in the cyber domain, taking the initiative against those who threaten our national security. The National Cyber Force plays a vital role in giving the UK that advantage,” he added. British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called the headquarters “a major investment in the North West, in defence innovation, and in keeping our country safe.” Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: “As hostile actors use cyberattacks to disrupt our way of life and cause us harm, our world class intelligence agencies ensure that we can tackle those threats head-on.” Ribble House’s ceremonial opening comes on the same day a House of Lords committee warned the country is “underprepared” for “potentially catastrophic risks” including cyberattacks from Russia, China and Iran. The committee said the government “appears complacent” and stressed the “need to move fast to turn things around.” No previous articleNo new articlesAlexander Martin is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. 2cj5p0.text: Microsoft says a software bug introduced in July caused last week's worldwide Microsoft 365 outage, triggering a cascading failure that left more than 80% of its networking gateway servers unresponsive. The nearly 24-hour outage on November 12 disrupted Microsoft 365 services worldwide, including Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams, and Copilot, leaving users unable to access their email and causing significant delays in message delivery. In a preliminary post-incident report shared in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center, the company said the outage was caused by three problems: a previously undetected software bug, increased traffic after a Microsoft Teams failover, and reduced server capacity. The incident began at 11:20 AM ET on Thursday, November 12, and continued until 11:10 AM ET the following day, when Microsoft confirmed that services were full restored. According to Microsoft, the software bug was introduced in July through an update developed for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. While the update had been deployed for more than three months without issues, it contained a bug that could overwhelm servers under certain traffic conditions, causing them to stop responding. Microsoft says its tests of the update did not detect the bug as it used less powerful testing hardware than the production servers. "Our normal load testing did not detect the latent issue because the traffic mix and SKUs used in our labs," Microsoft explained in its preliminary report. "The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware; whereas our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The bug was eventually triggered after Microsoft Teams automatically switched to the networking infrastructure used by Exchange Online approximately 15 hours before the outage, increasing traffic on those servers. Microsoft Teams also experienced a separate outage earlier that day, but it is unclear whether the two incidents are related. To make matters worse, Microsoft says nearly 14% of the gateway's server capacity was already offline due to an unrelated issue. While the infrastructure had sufficient capacity to handle the reduction, the combination of increased traffic and reduced capacity triggered the software bug. As servers stopped responding, Microsoft's systems redirected users to other available servers, which also became overwhelmed by the additional traffic and failed as well. "In less than two hours, the previously unknown defect was encountered across our fleet and rendered them unresponsive. At its lowest, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive," explained Microsoft. Microsoft says safeguards designed to prevent problems from spreading between regions also failed to contain the cascading outages, allowing the disruption to spread worldwide. While other Microsoft 365 services, like Teams, OneDrive, and SharePoint, could switch to alternative infrastructure and recover earlier, Exchange Online could not make the same switch, leaving users unable to access their mailboxes. Microsoft says recovery was difficult because restarting affected servers caused them to be quickly overwhelmed again by backed-up traffic. After identifying the bug, Microsoft engineers developed a fix and deployed it across affected servers, allowing services to stabilize throughout Friday. Microsoft confirmed that active customer impact had ended by 11:10 AM ET on November 13. The company says it has since increased capacity, improved monitoring, and added safeguards to prevent traffic redirection from triggering similar cascading failures. In a separate statement on X, Charles Lamanna, Microsoft's executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform, apologized for the disruption. "We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations," Lamanna said. Microsoft says its investigation is continuing, with a final post-incident report expected later this week. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. wlydl.text: Ticket seller Fandango Media is notifying customers about a data breach that exposed payment card details entered on its checkout pages. The company says the details were exposed between October 8 and 11, and it impacts customers who made purchases through its official website. Card skimmer code injected into Fandango’s checkout page intercepted payment card details entered when placing orders, sending the data to hackers. Fandango Media is a major U.S. online movie ticketing platform. It sells tickets through its website and app for 31,000 U.S. cinema screens, including at AMC, Regal, and Cinemark. The company also operates the popular movie review website Rotten Tomatoes. “Our investigation identified evidence that an unauthorized party could access payment card information associated with certain transactions on our checkout page from October 8-11, 2026,” reads the notification to customers. “Fandango determined on October 30, 2026 that your information may have been impacted in this incident.” The company says the following data types may have been exposed: Payment card number CVV (verification code) Expiration date Billing ZIP (postal code) Email address Fandango says the incident did not expose names, government-issued identity information, Social Security Numbers (SSNs), or any other account information. However, the information compromised in the incident could be used for unauthorized purchases on online stores. To reduce the risk to affected customers, Fandango is offering two years of free IDX credit and dark web monitoring, as well as identity theft recovery services, with an enrollment deadline of February 13, 2027. Fandango says it has now fixed the issue on its checkout page, investigated with outside cybersecurity specialists, and is currently unaware of any cases of fraud leveraging the stolen data. The company has not shared the number of affected customers. BleepingComputer has contacted Fandango to learn more, and we will update this post with their response once received. Users who bought movie tickets from Fandango during the exposure window should monitor their statements and account activity closely, and report any unauthorized purchases to their card issuer. One way to protect payment card details is to use one-time virtual cards when making online purchases. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 1ee8kv2.text: Compromised passwords and gaps in multi-factor authentication (MFA) remain common ways attackers gain access to sensitive systems. For law enforcement agencies handling criminal justice information (CJI), protecting against these threats is also a matter of CJIS compliance. The FBI's latest CJIS Security Policy sets clear requirements for password management and MFA. these are Priority 1 (P1) controls, so must be implemented immediately to comply. But this can be challenging, particularly across the complex IT environments that are common in law enforcement. This guide contains practical tips to help agencies meet the latest requirements, strengthen their defenses against credential-based attacks, and make ongoing compliance easier to manage. 1. Enforce Stronger Minimum Password Lengths CJIS requires user-selected passwords to be at least eight characters long, or six characters if generated by a credential service provider or verifier using an approved random number generator. However, we recommend going beyond these minimums and encouraging passphrases of at least 15 characters. Longer passwords are generally harder to crack, and passphrases can be easier to remember than shorter passwords with complex combinations of symbols and numbers. CJIS doesn't require traditional complexity rules, so focus on length and strength rather than arbitrary character requirements. 2. Block Weak and Compromised Passwords Agencies must maintain a list of commonly used, predictable, and compromised passwords. This should include passwords exposed in previous breaches, dictionary words, sequential characters, and context-specific terms such as usernames or agency names. CJIS requires agencies to update this list at least quarterly, and whenever organizational passwords are suspected of being compromised. Solutions like Specops Password Policy with Breached Password Protection can simplify this process with CJIS-aligned password policy templates. You can create an unlimited custom dictionary of blocked words unique to your agency, with granular controls for blocking weak constructions. Importantly, the Breached Password Protection feature delivers continuous screening against a growing database of more than six billion compromised passwords. 3. Reset Passwords Quickly and Give Users Clear Feedback Agencies must force a password change whenever there's evidence that a credential has been compromised. Don't rely solely on scheduled password changes to address exposed credentials. You must also check existing passwords against the breach list at least quarterly. More regular checks can help identify compromised credentials earlier, giving IT teams an opportunity to respond before attackers exploit them. CJIS also requires users to select a new password immediately whenever compromise is suspected. When a user does need to create or reset a password, rather than displaying a generic error message, provide clear, real-time feedback that helps users understand what makes a password weak and how to improve it. Specops Password Policy delivers that support, making it easier to create strong, memorable passwords while reducing frustration and unnecessary help desk requests. 4. Protect Passwords in Transit and At Rest Password security doesn't end with enforcing strong credentials. CJIS also requires passwords to be transmitted over encrypted, authenticated channels to prevent interception and man-in-the-middle attacks. When stored, passwords must be salted and hashed using a suitable one-way key derivation function, making them more resistant to offline cracking if an authentication database is compromised. Agencies should review how their applications and authentication systems handle credentials to ensure these protections are in place. 5. Require MFA For All Privileged and Non-Privileged Accounts CJIS requires MFA for both privileged and non-privileged organizational accounts. Don't focus solely on administrator accounts. Standard user accounts can also give attackers access to sensitive data or provide a foothold for further attacks. Review your accounts and access policies to identify where MFA is missing, including accounts belonging to employees and contractors. 6. Extend MFA Across All Relevant Access Methods CJIS requires MFA for local, network, and remote access. Agencies should review authentication across their environment, ensuring that all systems that touch CJI are adequately protected. ppq7u.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 16, 2026Agentic AI / Cyber Attacks Google on Monday revealed that adversarial use of artificial intelligence (AI) by threat actors has gone beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity. In tandem, threat actors are leveraging the power and capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and agentic frameworks to automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as observed in the case of PaperCut NG/MF flaws earlier this September. The abuse of open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks is seen as a way to "automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions," Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a report shared with The Hacker News. The tech giant said the adoption represents a paradigm shift in which cyber attacks take place at machine speed, allowing the operations to be scaled significantly by chaining together varied attack paths even if the underlying mechanics remain the same. A number of threat actors have been observed experimenting with these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated and suspected espionage actors aligned with China. "These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation," Google said. Another key area of misuse revolves around automating labor-intensive tasks like vulnerability analysis and proof-of-concept (POC) weaponization using LLM-driven pipelines, allowing threat actors to collapse the window between patch disclosure and active exploitation. "Threat actors may find it more efficient to use LLMs to rapidly weaponize patched n-day vulnerabilities, as they can focus research on a finite set of source materials: comparing source code versions (including from pre-release or preview channels), and examining release notes, security research, and POC code related to specific flaws," Google added. Simultaneously, threat actors are also targeting AI infrastructure to illicit profit from LLMjacking attacks by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised enterprise environments, and then reselling the access through underground proxy services like APIMart and JetNight at discounted prices, otherwise known as LLM mixers. The findings show that the emergence of open-source frameworks have further lowered the barrier to entry, enabling bad actors to easily integrate new exploits, autonomously scale attacks, and mount convincing phishing campaigns, further compressing attack timelines. This includes a Chinese-language phishing platform called Jieyou that has integrated an LLM chatbot assistant to allow customers to configure phishing panels and modify existing templates using natural language commands without necessarily having the technical expertise to do so. "The evolution of the Jieyou platform highlights a growing industry trend where PhaaS providers leverage LLMs as a modular force multiplier," Google said. "Rather than manually editing payloads, low-skilled affiliates can now utilize natural language through the chatbot to dynamically customize pretext lures and phishing interfaces on the fly."

Although AI was initially used experimentally in the attack flow, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) has observed its large-scale adoption by both financially motivated and state-sponsored threat groups. A notable example is the use of CAIRN, an open-source multi-agent penetration-testing framework, in an attack against the U.S. aerospace sector, and suspected North Korean hackers using Claude Code to deliver malware. The researchers estimate that in the next three months threat actors will be able to launch unsophisticated attacks that require "little to no human interaction" and rely mostly on multiple AI agents. Their projection is that "sophisticated, fully autonomous" agentic attacks are likely to emerge in the next six months. Evolution of AI use in cyberattacks Source: Google In an advisory last week, the FBI warned that multiple threat actors started weaponizing the ARTEX AI pentesting framework since August and launched attacks against organizations in the financial, government, technology, defense, healthcare, and other sectors. Using AI to find and exploit flaws Google says attackers now systematically abuse open-source pentesting suites to run fully automated attacks, including ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and HexStrike AI. Attackers used these frameworks to carry out adaptive attacks against internet-exposed endpoints vulnerable to low-complexity flaws for which large language models (LLMs) could easily build exploits. In one example GTIG highlights in its AI Threat Tracker report, hackers used a multi-agent system called ‘exploit_agent’ to fully automate vulnerability finding and exploitation in attacks targeting French media, entertainment, and education websites. “In the past quarter, GTIG identified threat actors using LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop for the first time,” Google says. “More specifically, GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework, dubbed exploit_agent, that integrates with multiple frontier and local LLMs.” Google discovered this framework from the attacker’s exposed staging server, which also included stolen victim data, reconnaissance information, webshells, and brute-forcing scripts. The system analyzes software updates on popular web apps to find signs of security flaws and automatically attempts to exploit them. Google warns that the deployment of such frameworks in attacks has dramatically decreased the time defenders have to patch their systems, while it also produces false leads. The researchers noted the recent example of PHP2Shell, where hundreds of purported proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, mostly AI-generated, appeared shortly after PHP announced the two flaws. This added a significant burden on defenders, as they had to verify the code and develop protections. Google reports AI is now routinely used in influence operations by state-backed groups, commercial vendors, and political networks. According to the researchers, LLMjacking has become a widespread problem, with attackers increasingly exploiting this new revenue stream at significant cost to affected organizations. Different stories, same problem: the things meant to protect us aren't always doing their job. Meanwhile, AI is making bug hunting faster, old flaws are still paying off, and attackers keep finding easy ways in. Some attacks take real skill. Others barely need any. This week's stories show both sides. Here's what happened. ⚡ Threat of the Week N-able 0-Days Exploited for Dropping Crypto Miners — A new set of vulnerabilities tracked as 4EverAble2Shell has come under active exploitation, with attackers exploiting it to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers. According to Huntback, the activity has successfully compromised 21 N-central servers across the U.S., South Africa, Canada, the U.K., Germany, France, and Sweden. Patches for the flaw are expected to be released N-able today. 🔔 Top News Compromised bee-js and Swarm Desktop Steal Swarm Wallet Keys — Threat actors compromised @ethersphere/bee-js, the JavaScript client for the Swarm storage network, with a new postinstall hook in version 13.3.0 that downloads a second stage responsible for stealing the Swarm node's wallet key and installing a backdoor. "On Linux and macOS, the backdoor is a Go remote shell," SafeDep said. "On Windows, it is a hidden ScreenConnect client that runs as SYSTEM." The same malicious code was subsequently distributed via Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 on GitHub. The activity has since been linked to a campaign called SleepyDuck (EtherDuck), which is known to spread malicious Solidity extensions through Open VSX. "The attacker controlled two Ethersphere GitHub accounts. GitHub activity logs attribute 13 pushes on November 6 to long-time maintainer nugaon," SafeDep added. "That day the attacker injected GitHub Actions workflows to steal CI credentials, and the attempts failed. Called SignDrop, it has been described as a Windows Common Log FileSystem (CLFS) authentication zero-day local privilege escalation flaw. "The vulnerability turns a defense into an attack surface," Cyderes said. "Microsoft added HMAC-based authentication codes to CLFS log files specifically to block the class of logic bugs caused by improper validation of CLFS data structures, which accounted for 19 of 24 CLFS CVEs over five years. SignDrop abuses the signing mechanism itself: it forces clfs.sys to create a .cnpf signature file as SYSTEM in an attacker-controlled location, producing a privileged file-creation primitive at an attacker-selected path. Because the resulting file retains attacker-accessible security attributes, the exploit reopens it and replaces the CLFS-generated content with an embedded payload DLL." Microsoft said it's investigating the reported vulnerability. 1feuwfd.text: Microsoft has reminded customers again that Windows Server 2016 will stop receiving security updates after it reaches the end of support in two months. This follows another warning issued in October, announcing the end of extended support for Windows Server 2016 and encouraging users to upgrade to Windows Server 2025. Windows Server 2016 reached general availability on October 12, 2016, one month after its official release at Microsoft's annual Ignite conference in September of that year. It also reached the end of mainstream support nearly 4 years ago, in January 2022, and extended support will end in roughly two months, on January 13, 2027. On the same date, the company will also stop support for all Windows Server 2016 Essentials features, including Remote Web Access and related Essentials-specific functionality. "On January 13, 2027, all editions of Windows Server 2016 will reach the end of extended support. The January 2027 Windows security update will be the last update provided during extended support," Microsoft said in a message center update. "After that date, monthly security updates will continue only for Windows Server 2016 devices enrolled in Extended Security Updates (ESU)." Windows Server 2025 upgrade Before Windows Server 2016 stops receiving security updates, Microsoft advised IT administrators to switch to Windows Server 2025, which started rolling out to Windows Insiders in January 2024 and reached general availability in November 2024. Admins who want to test Windows Server 2025 before deploying it across their organization can get a free 180-day trial via the Microsoft Evaluation Center. Windows Server 2025 is the latest Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) release for Windows Server, and it will reach the end of mainstream support in November 2029, with an additional five years of extended support until November 14, 2034. More information about Windows servicing dates is available on the Windows Lifecycle FAQ page or via the Lifecycle Policy search tool. 1ur43wb.text: Six flaws in Danfoss AK-SM800A refrigeration controllers could let a remote attacker take over a controller without logging in, Dutch security consultancy Midnight Blue said earlier this week. No patch is available, and the researchers say the newest firmware, version 5.4.0, does not fix the flaws. Government cybersecurity agencies in Belgium, Ireland and Germany told operators this week to take the controllers' management interfaces off the internet. For a controller left on the internet, updating the firmware, changing default passwords or turning on Strict mode is not enough on its own, the Belgian and Irish agencies said. Strict mode is a login protection that requires encrypted connections and session tokens, but one of the six flaws is in the gateway that enforces it. The AK-SM800A runs a store's fridges and freezers, and maintenance firms can manage it remotely. Such controllers were targeted in attacks in France starting October 11, and in a second wave across Europe that began last week. The attacks caused unwanted defrost cycles and destroyed stock. Germany's federal IT security agency, the BSI, says in a security notice that the AK-SM800A was involved in earlier incidents in which refrigeration units in several countries were tampered with. The agency has no information about any exploitation of the six new flaws, and neither other agencies nor researchers link the flaws to those incidents. The researchers examined firmware version 5.3.2, then the newest, and say every version up to and including it is affected. No CVE identifiers have been assigned. The researchers are keeping technical details private while they work on disclosure with Danfoss, the Danish company that makes the controllers. The vendor lists software package 5.4.0, dated November, as its newest release for the AK-SM800A. Its 5.4.0 readme and November update guide cover upgrade steps, and the guide adds a stricter password rule. Neither mentions a fix for any vulnerability. In a follow-up statement carried by trade publication Cooling Post, the researchers said 5.4.0 does not patch the flaws: "It's not really possible either because according to the file timestamp this firmware was likely built on October 29, before the second wave of cyber attacks and well before our vulnerability reports." The German agency first said in a press release this week that 5.4.0 was not affected. Later the same day, it changed that in a corrected statement: it cannot rule out for now that 5.4.0 is affected. The vendor's advisory page lists no advisory for the six flaws as of today, and no date for a fix has been published. Midnight Blue researcher Carlo Meijer found the six flaws in less than an hour of manual review, using firmware the vendor offers for download, and described them in a technical write-up. Five of the flaws are in web request handlers that do not require a login, inside a program that runs as root. Through one of them, the researchers ran code as root on older firmware, version 3.3.0, and they found the same bugs in 5.3.2. Strict mode closes almost all of the controller's web attack surface to users who have not logged in, including the flaw used in that demonstration. The sixth flaw is in the gateway that enforces Strict mode, a separate program that blocks every request except the login until a user has logged in. When the researchers ran firmware 5.3.2 in an emulator with Strict mode on, that flaw crashed the gateway. The crash could be turned into code execution with more work, the researchers say, and the gateway lacks basic exploit defenses such as stack canaries. With code running as root, an attacker could change the controller's settings, start defrost cycles and hide that activity from its logs. The controllers do not use secure boot, the researchers found, so an attacker could plant code that survives a factory reset and a firmware update. An attacker could also make a controller unusable until it is replaced. The researchers say the code almost certainly holds more flaws like these, and they call patching flaws one by one or turning on Strict mode "a misallocation of scarce security and personnel resources." What Operators Can Do Removing internet exposure must not wait for a patch, and it is needed even where firmware is current and Strict mode is on, the Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium says. The Belgian advisory and a similar Irish advisory recommend these steps: Find every controller whose management interface can be reached from the internet, including through a 4G or 5G modem, and remove that exposure. Give remote access only through a secure VPN or a protected internal network. Allowing only a service company's IP addresses through a firewall is a short-term measure. Check temperature setpoints, defrost schedules, alarm settings, user accounts and remote-access settings for changes you did not make. The German agency adds that anyone who suspects a compromise should change all credentials and check that equipment connected to the controller works properly. Before cutting off the data a controller sends to its refrigeration service company, operators should check contract and insurance terms, the Belgian advisory says. They should also set up protected remote access so that monitoring can continue. Danfoss's own update guide says the AK-SM800A should not be directly reachable from the public internet, adding: “This recommendation applies to all software versions, including those with Strict Mode enabled.” Ireland's National Cyber Security Centre also advises running the latest supported firmware, changing default passwords and turning on Strict mode, but says operators should not rely on those steps alone. Danfoss told Cooling Post on October 12 that most units hit in France were either older models that no longer receive updates or current AK-SM800A units running outdated firmware. The vendor fixed earlier flaws in the AK-SM800A in 2023 and 2025, including login bypass and command injection bugs. Version 5.3.2, which the researchers examined, is newer than all of those fixes.

gqzna8.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 16, 2026Threat Intelligence / Endpoint Security Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new variant of CoffeeLoader, a malware designed to deliver additional payloads to infected machines. "On launch, the NSIS-based installer executable dropped a file named '7z.dll' into a temporary directory and ran it through rundll32.exe," Kaspersky said in an analysis published today. "The '7z.dll' file was a patched version of the original library of the popular 7-Zip archiver. Part of its code had been replaced with malicious self-decrypting shellcode that turned out to be a new version of the Armoury packer." CoffeeLoader was first documented by Zscaler ThreatLabz in March 2025, detailing its use of the Armoury packer to resist analysis and ultimately run Rhadamanthys shellcode. The malware is assessed to share source code similarities with another loader family tracked as SmokeLoader. Malware packed with Armory uses file names like "ArmouryAIOSDK.dll" and "ArmouryA.dll," with the packer hijacking some of the original Armoury Crate functionality with self-decrypting shellcode. Notably, the shellcode extracts code that executes a decryption routine on a system's GPU by making use of the OpenCL library. The end goal is to install CoffeeLoader, establish persistence, and execute it by injecting it into a newly created "dllhost.exe" process. The latest version of the packer continues to use the GPU, but replaces OpenCL with the OpenGL library. In addition, the new version of the packer delivers intermediate shellcode instead of a DLL. This shellcode serves as a downloader responsible for fetching the main CoffeeLoader malware. "To establish persistence, the Trojan copies '7z.dll' to subfolders of %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%," Kaspersky said. "The Run registry key is used for autorun. The subfolder, library, and registry value are named with eight hexadecimal digits generated from system volume information." "To protect itself, the downloader creates a registry key that prevents the user from disabling autorun through Task Manager." Once persistence is successful, the malware launches one of the legitimate processes (e.g., "dllhost.exe," "WerFault.exe," "svchost.exe," "OpenWith.exe," or "AtBroker.exe") and then injects itself into it, after which the malware shellcode is downloaded from a hard-coded command-and-control (C2) server. The shellcode then decrypts and runs the CoffeeLoader payload. It supports the same three commands to run the next-stage malware from the C2 server - Injecting it into a process Saving it to disk as an executable and then running it Saving it as a DLL and then running it via "rundll32.exe" As for how CoffeeLoader is distributed, it takes place via Retadup, a Windows computer worm that was disrupted by French law enforcement authorities in August 2019. The malware, which spreads via infected USB drives, has been used to drop additional payloads like cryptocurrency miners, the Stop ransomware, and the Arkei password stealer. "Two years ago, someone began re-registering the domain names that Retadup had used as C2 servers and using them to issue commands to download third-party malware," Kaspersky said. "At first, this was the SmokeLoader downloader packed using the 32-bit version of Armoury, but in early 2025, the same servers started serving CoffeeLoader." It remains unclear whether the worm's author or some other threat actor was instrumental in bringing the C2 servers back online. Kaspersky said it blocked around 15,000 systems from being infected with the resurrected version of the worm, most of them located in Peru, Angola, Russia, and Bolivia.

133et5f.text: Coles Group Limited, Australia's second-largest retailer, is investigating what it described as a "cyber security incident" that has not impacted the company's stores. Founded in 1914, Coles now employs over 115,000 people, manages a network of more than 1,800 retail outlets, and operates the Flybuys loyalty program with over nine million active members. In a statement issued earlier today, the company said that it's now working with external experts to secure its systems and added that it has yet to find evidence that the attackers stole customer, employee, or supplier data from compromised systems. "Coles Group Limited is currently investigating a cyber security incident. Based on the findings of our investigation to date, we have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles' systems," the retail giant said. "Coles is working with the Australian Cyber Security Centre and will continue to engage with appropriate agencies and regulators as investigations continue. Coles is also working with global cyber security experts to contain and secure the Coles IT environment." It also noted that customers can shop as normal, as Flybuys accounts, Coles Plus, Coles Plus Delivery or QuiteLike subscriptions, and Coles stores and online outlets have not been affected by the cyberattack. However, it added that it is aware of Liquorland click-and-collect issues affecting a small number of customers. While it didn't link this to the incident, the company advised customers to be suspicious of any messages requesting personal data and recommended using unique passwords. "We advise everyone to take basic online precautions and recommend remaining vigilant to suspicious links, attempts to solicit personal information from you (including by email, phone, text, or post) and potential scam activity," it added. "We recommend you regularly update your password with a strong, unique password for your account and not reusing the same password across multiple services." Coles has not yet said when it discovered the incident or whether the attackers have made a ransom demand, and no major threat group has claimed the attack. 4bupgm.text: Anthropic recently rolled out Claude Mythos 5.2 to selected partners and Fable 5.2 to regular users, with improvements to coding and reasoning. But we also noticed some interesting cybersecurity changes. Anthropic describes Mythos 5.2 as its "most capable model for cybersecurity engineering," which means it's now ahead of Fable 5.2 in security research. However, that doesn't mean Fable 5.2 misses out on security restrictions, as it does come with cybersecurity safeguards, which block most potentially dangerous hacking activities. According to Anthropic, Mythos 5.2 beats Fable 5.2 at finding vulnerabilities, reproducing them, and developing fixes. This makes sense, as Mythos is designed for organizations working on advanced cybersecurity tasks. The company also shared some numbers. For example, Anthropic's CVE Rediscovery evaluation found that the Mythos 5.2 model can detect 10.2% more vulnerabilities than Claude Opus 5.5 and 14.4% more than Mythos 5.1. Moreover, a security company told Anthropic that "one in six confirmed bugs" identified by Mythos 5.2 had been missed by every other frontier model it tested. Claude Fable 5.2 blocks most high-risk cybersecurity tasks Although Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are based on the same underlying parent model, there are obvious differences, and it's totally due to their intended use cases. Unlike Mythos, Anthropic applied additional cybersecurity and biology safeguards to Fable so it can be made available to regular users. These safeguards block high-risk activities, including "penetration testing, exploit generation" and certain vulnerability research tasks involving binary analysis. If Anthropic detects high-risk activity, it will automatically switch to Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity-related responses. We've had those restrictions with Fable 5.1 as well, and at one point, it was starting to get annoying because Anthropic would block even normal requests. I've personally experienced unnecessary blocks when using Fable 5.1. For example, when I asked Fable 5.1 to log in to my droplet on AWS, it switched me to Opus 4.8, stating that it detected high-risk activity, even though Fable was the model that originally configured the AWS account via API. Thankfully, Fable is getting better at this. Anthropic says it has reduced unnecessary blocks by approximately 60% for cybersecurity requests compared with Fable 5.1. Anthropic observed "about 60% fewer in cybersecurity" during early testing across Claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork. Anthropic also tested Mythos 5.2 against sandbox escape attempts, where an AI agent tries to access files or credentials outside its permitted environment. Anthropic also admits that its evaluations cannot catch every potential failure before release, particularly as models become increasingly capable of recognizing when they are being tested. 13sbva5.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 16, 2026United States A financially motivated threat activity cluster tracked as REF3364 has been attributed to a Linux-focused cryptocurrency mining operation that tampers with the readings used to detect high GPU workloads. Central to the intrusion is a toolkit called SANSAR, a Rust-based orchestrator that receives commands over the TOR anonymity network to manage CPU and GPU miners. The activity was observed in late October 2026. "The threat actor also deployed a kernel rootkit to hide selected processes and files, an NVIDIA Management Library (NVML) wrapper to falsify GPU readings, and a separate backdoor named netns," Elastic Security Labs said in a report published last week. "This backdoor retrieves its C2 [command-and-control] address from an Ethereum smart contract before connecting to the server directly." In the attack chain documented by the company, initial access is said to have been achieved via an exposed Ray job agent, allowing the threat actor to execute commands. This includes jobs running the NVIDIA System Management Interface (nvidia-smi) to capture and exfiltrate the GPU inventory to an external server. Subsequently, the attacker submitted a Python reverse shell job that connected to a remote listener, after which an SSH key was added to that account's authorized_keys file to establish persistent access. "After obtaining root, the actor staged the toolkit under /opt/vadi_, built the acpi_thermal_mgr kernel module through Dynamic Kernel Module Support (DKMS) and added an initramfs loader," security researcher Salim Bitam said. "An initramfs is a temporary root file system loaded into RAM during early boot, before Linux switches to its normal root filesystem. The module and loader are stored in the boot image on disk, so the rootkit can load again when the host boots with that image." The installation also delivers a modified NVML wrapper that filters process information and changes GPU telemetry to evade detection. Specifically, the altered wrapper hooks NVML calls used by monitoring tools such as nvidia-smi to report GPU utilization as 0%. In addition, temperature and power readings are substituted with random values between 36 to 46 degree Celsius (96.8 to 114.8 degree Fahrenheit) and 100 to 200 watts. Also delivered are the following payloads - sansar, used for TOR C2, launching or stopping the miner, miner configuration updates, connection management, spawning interactive shells, launching an IPv4 TCP SYN traffic task against a specified address and port, and NVML-hook maintenance kurt (XMRig version 6.25.0), the miner selected by sansar's CPU branch tilki (SRBMiner-MULTI version 3.6.9), the miner selected by sansar's GPU branch lyrebird, a legitimate pluggable transport proxy for TOR acpi_thermal_mgr.ko, a Linux rootkit used for process, directory, and socket-list concealment netns, an Ethereum-assisted backdoor Once launched, SANSAR first performs an anti-debugging check by reading the value of TracerPid and exits if it's non-zero. TracerPid indicates the Process ID (PID) of the process currently tracing or debugging the target process. It then reaches out to an onion service ("efxisnqldelyr5ra25oqfrsut54b34g26e7zrsiuupsoekjof2gho2id[.]onion") for C2 communication via Arti, receiving commands, collecting host and GPU information, and fetching the miner status. The main responsibility of SANSAR is to supervise the mining process and launch the appropriate miner executable based on the miner type (i.e., CPU or GPU) specified in the C2 response message. The "acpi_thermal_mgr.ko" kernel rootkit, on the other hand, uses Function Tracer (ftrace) to conceal cryptomining activity on Linux systems by hiding processes, files, and socket entries. It achieves this by intercepting system calls to directory listings, file access, and process termination signals, removing matching records or blocking requests for those hidden processes and files by returning the message "No such file or directory" or "No such process." The other main component of the operation is the netns backdoor that's registered as a systemd service. It's used to retrieve a controller IPv4 address by sending requests to an embedded contract (0x43eb291f56688c63c93e8a93c4591fc997cf6349) and then sets up a plain TCP connection to that address on port 8080 to open a reverse-shell connection to the specified host and port in the C2 response. It's not clear who is behind the operation, but Elastic said it found Turkish language comments in the rootkit's source code. "Organizations expanding GPU infrastructure for AI and LLM workloads should check who can submit jobs and whether GPU monitoring libraries have been modified, as cryptojacking can divert compute capacity from legitimate workloads and increase operating costs," Elastic said.

znf9bd.text: An 11-year-old Linux kernel vulnerability, dubbed NoisyTCP, affects almost all Linux distributions and lets attackers crash systems running Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers with default configurations. According to Hyunwoo Kim, the security researcher who discovered it, this pre-authenticated remote corruption flaw (tracked as CVE-2026-99288) stems from a NULL pointer dereference weakness in the Linux kernel's TCP networking subsystem. Unauthenticated attackers can trigger it remotely via maliciously crafted TCP packets that exploit the timing between SYN cookie handling and socket hashing to crash the kernel and operating system on targeted servers. However, while CVE-2026-99288 exploits cause a kernel panic and take down the host, they don't allow threat actors to alter data or gain arbitrary code execution. Kim added that although attackers can exploit this vulnerability against any Linux system that receives TCP packets directly and runs Nginx, Apache, or an SSH server, "the race window is narrow, so triggering it against a quiet bare-metal server can take a long time." "Due to a race condition during lockless socket lookups, recycled socket memory can be accessed before it is properly initialized and hashed. A remote attacker could exploit this issue by generating network traffic that drives socket reuse, triggering a NULL pointer dereference and kernel crash that results in a Denial of Service (DoS)," the Red Hat security team explained. "To trigger this vulnerability, a stale ehash lookup and the freeing and reallocation of an existing request socket must proceed concurrently in different RX contexts. Packet processing has to be spread out by using the difference in receive hash between IPv4 fragments and regular TCP packets, so it can be triggered against servers that have two or more RX queues, or where RPS distributes packets across multiple CPUs," the researcher said. While a CVE-2026-99288 patch is already available and a fix was already merged into the mainline Linux kernel two weeks ago, the researcher advised those who can't apply it or upgrade immediately to disable SYN cookies (which will unfortunately lower protection against SYN flood attacks) and serialize to a single RX queue to block the race required for successful exploitation. In May, Kim also disclosed Dirty Frag, a Linux local privilege escalation flaw that chains RxRPC (CVE-2026-43500) and xfrm-ESP (CVE-2026-43284) page-cache write flaws to gain root access on major distributions, including Ubuntu, Red Hat Enterprise Linux, CentOS Stream, and Fedora. More recently, in July, he also disclosed Januscape, a 16-year-old Linux kernel vulnerability that enables attackers to escape a virtual machine and run arbitrary code on the host. 1duvvvw.text: Microsoft has released emergency out-of-band updates to fix Windows activation and licensing failures caused by this month's security updates. As the company confirmed in a Wednesday service alert, this known issue affects organizations that use the Software Licensing Management Tool (SLMGR) command-line tool to automate Windows activation and licensing processes. However, Microsoft said that enterprise customers who don't use SLMGR for licensing management and have the KMS client key installed in their image are unaffected. "Devices that are already activated remain activated. Customers whose devices already have the appropriate KMS client key and KMS configuration, and who do not need to run the affected Slmgr.vbs commands, are not expected to be affected," the company noted. On Friday, Microsoft released multiple emergency Windows updates to fix the bug on the following client (Windows 10 21H2/22H2 and Windows 11 23H2) and server (Windows Server 2019/2022/2025) platforms: Windows Server 2025: KB5136489 Windows Server 2022: KB5136487 Windows Server 2019 and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2019: KB5136490 Windows 11, version 23H2: KB5136483 Windows 10, version 22H2 ESU and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021: KB5136493 For Windows Server 2025, Windows Server 2022, Windows Server 2019, and Windows 10, the out-of-band updates are available only through the Microsoft Update Catalog. The Windows 11, version 23H2 optional OOB update is available through Windows Update and the Microsoft Update Catalog and can be installed from Settings > Windows Update > Advanced options > Optional updates to download. "This cumulative update includes the improvements from the November 2026 Windows security update," Microsoft added. "For complete guidance and installation instructions, see the relevant KB articles." In January, Microsoft resolved a similar issue that was causing Windows license migration failures during upgrades because impacted devices couldn't register with the Windows Activation server for digital licenses. Last week, it also acknowledged that Windows updates released since the October Patch Tuesday are triggering SQL Server performance and stability issues and that the November 2026 Windows 11 security updates fail to install on systems with the October 2026 preview update.
